title: A Ram, a Goat, and a Cruel King
overview: Daniel sees a vision of animals fighting that, as the angel Gabriel explains, traces the fall of Persia to Greece and the rise of a later Greek king who would attack the Jewish people and their temple.

parts.label: Setting by the river (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: This vision is dated near the end of Babylon's rule, while Daniel still serves there. In the vision, not in body, he finds himself at Susa, a city that later became a royal capital of Persia, the empire the vision begins with.

parts.label: The ram and the goat (vv. 3-8)
parts.note: The angel later explains the two-horned ram as Media and Persia, and the taller horn that grew later is Persia, which came to outshine Media. The goat from the west is Greece, and its great horn is widely taken as Alexander the Great, who conquered Persia at astonishing speed, died young at the height of his power, and whose empire split into four kingdoms.

parts.label: The small horn grows (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: Most scholars identify this horn as Antiochus IV, a Greek king based in Syria who in the 160s BC banned Jewish worship, stopped the daily temple offerings and defiled the temple. Throwing down the stars pictures his attack on God's people and his defiance of God himself, and the text ties this to rebellion without saying whose, so some read it as the people's unfaithfulness and others as the king's own wrongdoing.

parts.label: How long? (vv. 13-14)
parts.note: Two heavenly beings ask how long the temple will be trampled, and the answer is 2,300 evenings and mornings. Scholars are unsure whether this means 2,300 days or 1,150 days counting evening and morning offerings separately, but the temple was in fact purified and rededicated in 164 BC, an event Jewish people still remember at Hanukkah.

parts.label: Gabriel explains (vv. 15-26)
parts.note: Gabriel names Media, Persia and Greece outright, then describes a fierce, scheming king who will destroy many and stand against God, yet be broken by no human hand, which fits accounts of Antiochus dying of illness rather than in battle. Daniel is told to seal up the vision because it concerns the distant future, though what sealing it and 'the time of the end' mean exactly is debated.

parts.label: Daniel overwhelmed (v. 27)
parts.note: Daniel is left sick and exhausted for days. He goes back to his work for the king, but he admits he still cannot make sense of what he saw.

disagreement: Christians differ over whether this vision was fully fulfilled in Antiochus IV or also points ahead to a final enemy of God at the end of history, and some traditions read the 2,300 days as years leading to a modern date.
think: What do you think it does to people living under oppression to be told their suffering has a set limit, even when they cannot yet see the end of it?
